overview.intro: The Sangam Age (c. 300 BCE - 300 CE) is the earliest well-documented chapter of south Indian history, named after the Sangams - academies of Tamil poets and scholars at Madurai - whose anthologies preserve its literature. This chapter studies the two key sources, the Tirukkural and the megaliths, then surveys Sangam society with special focus on the position of women, and the economy of agriculture and trade.

blocks.text: South of the Vindhyas, three kingdoms - the Cheras (Kerala), the Cholas (Kaveri delta) and the Pandyas (Madurai) - flourished between c. 300 BCE and 300 CE. Their courts hosted the Sangam poets, whose anthologies (Ettutogai, Pattupattu and others) and the grammar Tolkappiyam form the literary corpus. The age also left megalithic burials across the peninsula, and its ports traded with Rome: from Roman coins found at Arikamedu to pepper exported in such quantity that Roman authors complain of the drain of gold to India.

Sources - Tirukkural. The Tirukkural by Tiruvalluvar is the crown of Tamil ethics: 1,330 short couplets in three books - virtue (aram), wealth (porul) and love (kamam). Its maxims on justice, kingship, friendship, agriculture ('the ploughmen are the axle of the world'), non-violence and the dignity of the trader reflect the values of Sangam society; it is a primary literary source for the age's ideals.

Sources - Megaliths. Across south India, the dead of this era were buried under megaliths - 'great stones': cists (stone boxes) sometimes with port-holes, dolmens (table stones), menhirs (upright pillars) and stone circles, often containing iron tools, black-and-red ware pottery, beads and, rarely, horse skeletons. These burials are the chief archaeological source: they prove iron technology, settled village life, and belief in afterlife, and their distribution marks the spread of settlement in the peninsula.

Society. Sangam literature divides the land into five tinais: kurinji (hills - hunting/honey), mullai (forest - pastoralism), marudam (riverine plains - plough agriculture), neydal (coast - fishing/salt) and palai (dry land - raiding). Society was organised by occupation rather than rigid birth-caste: rulers and warriors (arasar), the vellalar landholders and uzhavar ploughmen, artisans and traders, and at the bottom the adimai (slaves). Family was patriarchal; the village (ur) was the basic unit, with larger assemblies (sabha/ur) managing affairs; hero-stones (nadukal/virakkal) commemorating fallen warriors show a martial ethos.

Position of women. Women in Sangam society held a comparatively honoured place. They could be educated and were poets in their own right - notably Avvaiyar, whose poems appear in Sangam anthologies; women's work in agriculture, weaving and rice-pounding was valued; the wife was the 'lamp of the home'. Chastity (karpu) was exalted as the supreme feminine virtue, and widows' remarriage was discouraged (unlike Vedic custom), but sati was not imposed. Royal women, e.g., the queens of the Chera king, appear in literature with dignity. Nevertheless, society remained patriarchal: inheritance and public power were largely male, and the ideal of karpu limited women's freedom.

Economy - agriculture. Agriculture was the backbone: the Kaveri delta rice-farms yielded two or three crops a year; the state built tanks, dams and canals (the Chola king Karikala is credited with embankments of the Kaveri). Paddy, sugarcane, cotton, pepper, ginger, turmeric and cardamom were grown; plough, irrigation channels and manuring were known. The vellalar class commanded the plough economy; land revenue and gifts of land to Brahmanas appear in later Sangam-era records. The Tirukkural's praise of the farmer - 'the ploughmen alone live independent... others follow' - shows agriculture's prestige.

Economy - trade. Trade was brisk, internal and overseas. Internally, towns like Madurai, Uraiyur, Puhar (Kaveripattinam) and Korkai held markets (angadi) with separate streets for different trades; barter and coins (Chera, Chola, Pandya punch-marked and Roman coins) circulated. Overseas: pepper, pearls from the Gulf of Mannar (Korkai), muslin, silk-cotton, sandalwood, spices and precious stones went west; Roman ships rode at Arikamedu (Poduke) - its excavations yielded Roman amphorae, lamps and coins of Augustus and Tiberius. Roman gold poured into Tamil ports; Yavana merchants settled in coastal colonies. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) lists these ports and goods.

blocks.text: Tirukkural vs Megaliths: Literary source (ethical couplets) versus archaeological source (burial monuments).
Kurinji vs Marudam: Hill eco-zone of hunting/honey versus riverine plains of plough agriculture.
Vellalar vs Adimai: Landed ploughmen at the top of the working order versus slaves/bonded labour at the bottom.

items: Calling the Sangam a royal assembly of kings - it was an academy of poets/scholars.
Attributing the Tirukkural to Kambar or any other poet - it is Tiruvalluvar's.
Saying Sangam society had the rigid four-fold varna system - occupation groups were more fluid.
Placing Arikamedu on the east coast wrongly - it is near Pondicherry (Poduke).
Claiming women had full equality - they were honoured but society remained patriarchal.

questions.prompt: The Sangam literature was chiefly composed in which language?
questions.explanation: The Sangams were academies of Tamil poets at Madurai.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming Sanskrit for all ancient Indian texts.

questions.prompt: Arikamedu is famous for the excavation of:
questions.explanation: Arikamedu (Poduke) proves Indo-Roman trade of the Sangam era.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing it with a purely megalithic site.

questions.prompt: Which Sangam woman poet's works appear in the anthologies?
questions.explanation: The others are Vedic women seers, not Sangam poets.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing Vedic rishikas with Sangam poets.

questions.prompt: Who authored the Tirukkural, and how many couplets does it contain?
questions.explanation: Divided into aram (virtue), porul (wealth) and kamam (love).

questions.answer: Huge stones used to build burial monuments - cists, dolmens, menhirs - often containing iron tools, pottery and beads.
questions.explanation: The chief archaeological source for the age.

questions.prompt: Name the three crowns (kingdoms) of the Sangam age with their capitals/ports.
questions.answer: Cheras (Vanji/Karur; ports Muziris and Tondi), Cholas (Uraiyur; port Puhar/Kaveripattinam), Pandyas (Madurai; port Korkai).
questions.explanation: King + capital + port for full marks.

questions.prompt: What evidence shows that the Sangam age traded with Rome?
questions.answer: Roman coins (Augustus, Tiberius) hoarded in Tamil lands; Roman amphorae, lamps and glass at Arikamedu; references to Yavana traders in Sangam poems; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea listing Tamil ports; Roman authors' complaints of gold drain to India for pepper and pearls.
questions.commonMistake: Citing only one type of evidence.

questions.prompt: Describe the position of women in Sangam society.
questions.answer: Women could be educated and were poets in their own right (Avvaiyar); they worked in agriculture, weaving and rice-pounding, and were honoured as the 'lamp of the home'. Chastity (karpu) was exalted as the supreme feminine virtue; widow remarriage was discouraged but sati was not imposed. Society remained patriarchal - inheritance and public power were largely male.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming full equality, or total subjection.

questions.prompt: Explain why agriculture prospered in the Sangam age.
questions.answer: The Kaveri delta's fertile alluvial soil supported paddy; kings built tanks, canals and embankments (Karikala's Kaveri bund is celebrated); iron ploughs and irrigation lifted yields; two or three crops a year became possible; the vellalar landholders commanded a stable labour force of uzhavar (ploughmen). The Tirukkural itself declares the ploughman the axle of the world, showing the prestige of agriculture. Surplus rice then fed trade and ports.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Tirukkural and the megaliths as sources of the Sangam age.
questions.answer: The Tirukkural is a literary source: Tiruvalluvar's 1,330 Tamil couplets on virtue, wealth and love, reflecting the age's ethics, economy and society in idealised verse. The megaliths are archaeological sources: stone burial monuments (cists, dolmens, menhirs) whose grave-goods - iron tools, black-and-red ware, beads, horse remains - prove iron technology, settled life and burial beliefs. The Kural gives values; the megaliths give material facts - the two together round out the picture.
questions.explanation: Nature (literary vs archaeological) + what each proves.

questions.prompt: Describe the economy of the Sangam age under the heads of agriculture and trade.
questions.answer: Agriculture: the chief occupation, concentrated in the fertile Kaveri delta (marudam zone); paddy the staple, with sugarcane, cotton, pepper, ginger, turmeric and cardamom; the state and kings built tanks, dams and canals - Karikala Chola's embankment of the Kaveri is famous; iron plough, manuring and irrigation supported two or three crops yearly; the vellalar landholders and uzhavar ploughmen formed the productive core, and the Tirukkural honoured the ploughman as the world's axle. Trade: internal trade ran through towns like Madurai, Uraiyur and Puhar, with separate market streets for trades, barter plus coins (Chera-Chola-Pandya issues and Roman coins); external trade flourished with Rome - pepper, pearls (Korkai), muslin, sandalwood and spices exported; Roman gold flowed in, as Roman coins and Arikamedu's amphorae and lamps prove; ports included Puhar, Korkai and Muziris; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea lists these exchanges; Yavana merchants settled in coastal colonies. Agriculture fed trade, and trade enriched the kingdoms.
questions.explanation: Cover crops, irrigation, land classes, internal + overseas trade with evidence.

questions.prompt: Which trade route change boosted Indo-Roman trade around 45 CE?
options: Discovery of the monsoon sea route (Hippalus)
questions.answer: Discovery of the monsoon sea route (Hippalus)
questions.explanation: Using monsoon winds, ships sailed direct - cutting time and cost.
questions.commonMistake: Not connecting monsoons to Roman trade.
